lines.text: But dearest—Did you not understand that I understood?
lines.note: Shows Elizabeth's early sense that Robert already understands her.

lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Flush's ecstatic welcome captures a vivid, private moment of home.

lines.text: My own dearest, let me say the most urgent thing first.
lines.note: Robert's urgent opening shows his care about her brothers' suspicions.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Elizabeth's sudden loss of Flush becomes a turning point in their week.

lines.text: Poor Flush—how sorry I am for you, my Ba!
lines.note: Robert's sympathy for Flush shows his tenderness during the crisis.

lines.text: It seems to me that you and I are at one upon the whole question,—only that I am your Flush, and he is mine.
lines.note: Elizabeth turns the dog-stealing argument into their private joke: 'I am your Flush, and he is mine.'

lines.text: Only a few words to tell you that Flush is found, and lying on the sofa, with one paw and both ears hanging over the edge of it.
lines.note: Flush lying on the sofa gives relief after the ransom ordeal.

lines.text: The sight of your letter, even, did not provoke the cloud—that was only the lesser joy, I thought, preceding the greater!
lines.note: Elizabeth's smile at Robert's 'grave man and woman' shows their playful shorthand.

lines.text: Dearest, you are a prophet, I suppose—there can be no denying it.
lines.note: The sudden family removal forces the marriage question into the open.

lines.text: I will go for a licence to-day and we can be married on Saturday.
lines.note: Robert's licence plan turns urgency into a concrete plan to marry.

lines.text: You have given me the highest, completest proof of love that ever one human being gave another.
lines.note: Robert's praise crowns the day they married.

lines.text: My own beloved, if ever you should have reason to complain of me in things voluntary and possible, all other women would have a right to tread me underfoot, I should be so vile and utterly unworthy.
lines.note: Elizabeth's answer to his wish to be better shows her gratitude after the wedding.

lines.text: I feel so as if I had slipped down over the wall into somebody’s garden—I feel ashamed.
lines.note: Her garden-wall image captures the strange new happiness of being married.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's last letter looks ahead to having only Robert to love her.
